rows.answer: PEP 572 introduces the notation ``NAME := expr`` for creating a way to assign to variables within an expression [5]. An alternative spelling using a left-facing arrow, ``EXPR -> NAME``, is also provided and inspired by languages such as R and Haskell [1][4]. The construct's formal name is "Assignment Expressions," though it may also be referred to as "Named Expressions" [5].
PEP 8 recommends using 4 spaces per indentation level [1].

The Python style guide recommends limiting all lines to a maximum of 79 characters [1]. For docstrings or comments, the limit should be reduced to 72 characters [1]. Teams may increase this limit up to 99 characters if they can reach an agreement on it [2].
The first aphorism in the Zen of Python is "Beautiful is better than ugly." [2]

For consistency, always use triple double quotes around docstrings [1]. When using triple-quoted strings, you should always use double quote characters to align with the docstring convention in PEP 257 [4]. If backslashes are present in your docstrings, use raw triple double quotes (r"""...) [1].

The symbol placed before a decorator expression above a function definition is `@`. This is shown in the syntax rule where `decorator` is defined as `'@' dotted_name [ '(' [arglist] ')' ] NEWLINE` [3]. Examples in the text also demonstrate this usage, such as `@decomaker(argA, argB, ...)` followed by a function definition [3].

An object needs the `__enter__()` and `__exit__()` methods to be used in a with statement [2]. These objects implementing that protocol are known as "context managers" [2]. The decorator `contextlib.contextmanager` can convert a generator function into such a context manager factory [1].

The proposed syntax `yield from <expr>` allows a generator to delegate part of its operations to another generator [1]. This expression is evaluated against an iterable, and if the iterator is a generator, it can execute a `return` statement whose value becomes the result of the `yield from` expression [5].
The configuration file that marks the root of a virtual environment is ``pyvenv.cfg`` [4].

A new module in the standard library called ``typing`` is introduced to provide a uniform namespace for static type checking [1]. This module defines fundamental building blocks such as ``Any``, ``Union``, and ``List`` for constructing types [1][3].

PEP 492 introduced the keyword `async` for declaring native coroutines using the `async def` syntax [1]. It also introduced the keyword `await` for suspending execution within those functions [1]. The proposal explicitly states that it is a `SyntaxError` to have `yield` or `yield from` expressions in an `async` function, distinguishing them from generator-based coroutines [1].
Formatted string literals are commonly called "f-strings" [1]. This name is derived from the leading character 'f' used to denote such strings, standing for "formatted strings" [1].

PEP 518 introduces a new configuration file for software packages to specify their build dependencies [3]. This file is expected to be used in the ``pyproject.toml`` format, where the ``[build-system]`` table stores build-related data [5]. An example of this configuration within a ``pyproject.toml`` file shows the ``requires`` key listing dependencies like "setuptools" [1].

PEP 526 adds syntax for variable annotations to Python [1]. This syntax is intended for adding typing to variables, parameters, and function returns alongside :pep:`484` and :pep:`526` [5]. It serves as a core part of the language to alleviate issues with distinguishing normal comments from type comments [4].

The `@dataclass` decorator generates `__init__` and `__repr__` methods by default when its parameters are set to `init=True` and `repr=True` [4]. This decorator is provided in the `dataclasses` module to post-process classes and add these generated methods [5].

A union of two types can be written using the ``|`` operator, such as ``int | str`` instead of ``Union[int, str]`` [1]. This syntax allows writing ``t | None`` or ``None | t`` instead of ``Optional[t]`` [1]. The proposal adds the ``type.__or__()`` operator to enable this notation [1].

A ``ParamSpec`` captures both positional and keyword accessible parameters [1]. It is designed to capture all three parameter categories (positional-only, positional-or-keyword, keyword-only) into a single higher-level primitive before they are split out afterward [2]. A given binding for a ParamSpec represents a set of function parameters, not the arguments passed at a call site [3].

Core project metadata is stored in the `[project]` table of `pyproject.toml` [3]. This table supports fields like `dependencies` and `optional-dependencies` for packaging tools [5]. The PEP also discusses specific sub-tables within this structure, such as `[project.urls]` (now suggested as `[project.project-urls]`) [4].
Structural pattern matching introduces the `match` statement [1].

The pattern ``_`` acts as a wildcard that always matches but does not bind any variables [2]. This special pattern is written as ``_`` and can be used to catch cases where all other patterns fail [2]. It may also appear in sequence patterns like ``(x, y, *_)`` to match remaining items without binding them [3].

The marker file named ``EXTERNALLY-MANAGED`` indicates that a Python installation is externally managed [1]. This file is specified to live in the ``stdlib`` directory in the default ``sysconfig`` scheme [1]. Its presence signifies that non-virtual-environment package installations are managed by an external means, such as a distro's package manager [1].
The `Self` type is added to the `typing` module. [1]

The soft keyword that starts the new type alias statement is ``type`` [1][2]. This keyword is introduced to define a scope for type parameters similar to ``class`` and ``def`` statements [1]. It is interpreted as a keyword only within the specific grammar rules for type aliases and generic class/function definitions [2].

PEP 703 proposes making the global interpreter lock ("GIL") optional in CPython [1]. This change allows Python code to run without the GIL and with necessary modifications to make the interpreter thread-safe [1].

Function annotations are stored in the function's ``__annotations__`` attribute [1]. This attribute is a mutable dictionary that maps parameter names to their evaluated annotation expressions [1]. The special key "return" within this dictionary holds the return value annotation if one was supplied [1].

PEP 3156 proposed a package named ``asyncio`` for asynchronous I/O support [1]. This proposal included a pluggable event loop and transport abstractions [1]. The document states that this is the concrete proposal missing from :pep:`3153` [1].

The developmental release segment consists of the string ``.dev``, followed by a non-negative integer value [3]. A version identifier that includes this segment is termed a "developmental release" [3]. This segment is ordered immediately before the corresponding release and any pre-releases with the same release segment [3].

The keyword ``yield`` turns an ordinary function into a generator function [3]. When a function contains a ``yield`` statement, it is called a generator function [3]. This makes ``yield`` a new keyword used inside functions to define generators [3].

The style guide recommends that class names normally use the CapWords convention [1]. For exceptions, which are classes, the same convention applies but with the suffix "Error" if the exception is an error [2]. Double leading underscores should generally be used only to avoid name conflicts in subclassed classes [5].

Comparisons to singletons like `None` should always be done with `is` or `is not`, never the equality operators [1][2]. The form `if foo is not None:` is preferred over `if not foo is None:` for readability [1]. Singletons such as `True`, `False`, and `None` are compared by identity rather than equality [3].

You can assign a value to a variable inside an `if` condition using assignment expressions with the syntax `if re.search(pat, text) as match:` [1]. This approach works effectively when the condition is based on the truthiness of the captured value, such as in regex matches or socket reads [1]. However, it is completely useless for more complicated cases where the condition involves a function comparison like `f(x) < 0` [1]. Additionally, this syntax does not provide any benefit to list comprehensions [1].

You should declare build dependencies in a new configuration file introduced by PEP 518, such as `pyproject.toml` [4]. This file is specifically used to specify what build dependencies are needed to execute the chosen build system [4]. While the file may also store other configuration details, it is the designated place for this purpose [3].

A Linux distribution can stop pip from installing into the system Python by shipping a marker file in the ``stdlib`` directory and placing distro-shipped packages in a location other than the default ``sysconfig`` scheme [4]. These actions signal that the interpreter's packages are managed externally, preventing ``pip install`` from modifying them by default [4]. Additionally, distributions can apply patches to pip to prevent it from deleting distro-installed packages, as Debian does [1].
